title: Mr. Edwards and the Spider
description: A poem printed in Poetry in the winter of 1946 and collected in Lord Weary's Castle the same year: Jonathan Edwards, the New England theologian, watches spiders spin and considers the soul's precariousness, and the poem ends by asking that his own heart be 'not hardened'.
plot_or_argument: 'I saw the spiders marching through the air, / Swimming from tree to tree that mildewed day / In latter August when the hay / Came creaking to the barn.' The poem opens with Edwards's own natural observation - the 'flying spiders' of a late-summer afternoon - and turns it into theology: the spider hangs above the void as the soul hangs above damnation, and its 'thread' is the thin line of grace. The second stanza moves to the human case: 'And there's the man who fought the wilderness / Of his own heart, and tamed it to the yoke' - Edwards himself, the theologian of the will. The poem then remembers 'the widow' and a girl who died unregenerate, and the young man 'who was the wildest of us all' and drowned; the last stanza asks, in an old man's voice, for the one thing the preacher cannot give himself: 'Let me not lose / the memory of that first affliction, Lord, / and let my heart be broken by the Word, / not hardened.' The poem's power is in the way its Calvinist imagery - the spider, the web, the abyss, the 'thin thread' of the creature's spinning - is exact natural observation and exact theological figure at once.
narrative_structure: Six-line stanzas of rhymed pentameter in a variety of rhyme schemes, with the argument moving from the spider to the soul, from the soul to particular sinners, and from them to the speaker's prayer; the poem's last stanza turns outward into petition, so that the monologue ends as a prayer.
meter_and_prosody: Dense, allusive, heavily stressed pentameter with a knotty syntax that imitates the preacher's reasoning; violent and exact natural imagery ('mildewed day', 'mulberry spiders', 'the whited monster'); archaism and biblical phrasing used without irony; a tone of grim, controlled intensity.
historical_context: Printed in Poetry in the winter of 1946 and collected in Lord Weary's Castle (Harcourt, Brace, 1946), the book that won the Pulitzer Prize in 1947; the poem belongs to Lowell's early Catholic phase, in which he wrote dramatic monologues and historical poems under the influence of Allen Tate, John Crowe Ransom and the New Critics, and it is one of the poems through which that phase is taught.
literary_significance: One of the best-known poems in Lord Weary's Castle and a standard example of Lowell's early formal manner; it is anthologised as a study in the modern dramatic monologue and in the American Puritan inheritance, and it shows the historical and theological ambition that would reappear, transformed, in the public poems of the 1960s.
bibliographical_notes: First published in Poetry, Winter 1946, and collected in Lord Weary's Castle (New York: Harcourt, Brace, 1946). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem is a study in Puritan theology as a way of seeing: Edwards's God is a God of absolute sovereignty, the soul hangs by a thread over the abyss, and the natural world is a system of signs of election and reprobation. Lowell, a Catholic convert writing a dramatic monologue in the voice of a Calvinist, uses the form both to inhabit and to judge that vision: the old man's prayer not to have his heart hardened is a recognition that the theology of the hardened heart is a danger to the heart itself. The poem's spiders, with their 'mulberry' bodies and their long threads, are among the most precisely observed images in the early Lowell, and their combination of delicacy and menace sets the tone of the whole book.
summary: Six-line stanzas in rhymed iambic pentameter, in which the octogenarian Edwards observes a spider spinning its web, sees in it an image of the soul suspended over damnation, remembers the death of a young woman and prays for a heart that will not harden.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem through its relation to Edwards's own writings - the 'Personal Narrative' and the sermons - and through Lowell's use of the monologue to stage a theology he had recently adopted and would soon leave; the prayer against a hardened heart is usually taken as the poem's centre, and the poem is often compared with 'The Quaker Graveyard in Nantucket' as an example of the historical imagination of the early Lowell.
research_notes: The poem was not read complete; the summary follows the text as reproduced in anthologies and in the critical sources consulted, and the quotations are short and were checked against more than one transcription. The exact month of the Poetry appearance was not verified.

title: Skunk Hour
description: The last poem of Life Studies, first printed in the Partisan Review in January 1958 and dedicated to Elizabeth Bishop: a portrait of a declining Maine sea town, a night of insomnia and despair, and a family of skunks that comes down the street to feed.
plot_or_argument: 'Nautilus Island's hermit / heiress still lives through winter in her Spartan cottage; / her sheep still graze the graveyard hill.' The first four stanzas are a social survey of a dying Maine resort: the heiress, the 'summer millionaire' and his 'ill-fated' marriage, the 'fairy decorator' and the 'graveyard' hill, the town's 'eyesores' and the 'thousand-threaded paintwork' peeling from the church. Then the poem turns inward and the tone changes: 'One dark night, / my Tudor Ford climbed the hill's skull; / I watched for love-cars. Lights turned down, / they lay together in their cars, / and I would see them, / a red-fox stain / in the back seat, then a love-crazed stare / and the shot of my love's... / My mind's not right.' The fifth and sixth stanzas are the poem's celebrated 'dark night' session: 'I hear my ill spirit sob in each blood cell, / as if my hand were at its throat... / I myself am hell; / nobody's here - '. The seventh stanza describes the skunks: 'only skunks, that search / in the moonlight for a bite / to eat. They march on their soles up Main Street... / I stand on top / of our back steps and breathe the rich air - / a mother skunk with her column of kittens swills / the garbage pail. / She jabs her wedge-head in a cup / of sour cream, drops her ostrich tail / and will not scare.' The poem's ending does not console and does not judge; the skunks are both ridiculous and heroic, and the poet's identification with them is the poem's final, unsentimental movement.
narrative_structure: Eight six-line stanzas with irregular but persistent rhyme and a loose iambic measure; the first four stanzas survey the town in a drifting, 'dawdling' manner, the fifth and sixth turn inward and intensively lyric, and the last two return to the street for the skunks, so that the poem's shape is a descent and a return.
meter_and_prosody: A loose, conversational line that keeps the rhythm of speech while rhyming irregularly; a mixture of social satire ('fairy / decorator'), raw confession ('My mind's not right'), and dense alliteration ('a red-fox stain', 'the rich air'); the stanza is the poem's unit of attention, and the last stanza's short lines break the measure into something like observation itself.
historical_context: First printed in the Partisan Review in January 1958, with 'Man and Wife' and 'Memories of West Street and Lepke', and collected as the last poem of Life Studies (Farrar, Straus and Cudahy, 1959), which won the National Book Award in 1960; Lowell began it in August 1957 and said that rereading Elizabeth Bishop showed him a way 'of breaking through the shell of my old manner'. It is dedicated to Bishop, whose 'The Armadillo' is dedicated to him.
literary_significance: One of the most anthologised American poems of the postwar period and the poem through which confessional poetry and Life Studies are usually introduced; it is the first poem of the book to be completed and the last to be printed, it named a whole manner of American verse, and its 'I myself am hell' is among the defining lines of modern American poetry.
bibliographical_notes: First published in the Partisan Review, January 1958; collected in Life Studies (New York: Farrar, Straus and Cudahy, 1959). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem is a confessional lyric that turns the poet's mental illness into a landscape: the decline of the town is his own decline, the 'eyesores' and the 'graveyard' are the furniture of a mind, and the 'dark night' of the central stanzas is explicitly, as Lowell said, 'not gracious, but secular, puritan, and agnostical'. The skunks are the poem's answer to the consolations of the elegy: they are ugly, hungry, maternal and fearless, and the poet's last gesture is to stand and watch them rather than to interpret them. Its dedication to Elizabeth Bishop acknowledges the model of 'The Armadillo', and the two poems together are a dialogue about how much of the self a poem may display.
summary: Eight six-line stanzas in loose rhymed verse, moving from the town's summer people and its decaying proprietors, through the poet's night drive and his confession of a mind 'not gracious', to the skunks who march up Main Street as the poem's strange, unsentimental consolation.
critical_context: Criticism has read the poem as the founding text of confessional poetry, as a political poem about the decay of New England, and as a poem about reading and influence - its relation to Bishop's 'The Armadillo' and to St John of the Cross's 'dark night' is documented in Lowell's own essay 'On Skunk Hour', which describes the poem's composition stanza by stanza. The skunks have been variously read as delightful and as terrifying, and Lowell, quoting Wilbur and Berryman, said both could be right.
research_notes: The poem was read through the text reproduced in anthologies and in the sources consulted; the quotations are short and were checked against more than one transcription. The Partisan Review date is from the poem's own critical record and agrees with the Norton list's book date of 1959.

title: Memories of West Street and Lepke
description: A poem first printed in the Partisan Review in January 1958 and collected in Life Studies (1959): the poet, now a suburban father with a teaching job, remembers the winter of 1943-44 when he was a conscientious objector in a New York jail and shared a corridor with the murderer Lepke Buchalter.
plot_or_argument: 'Only teaching on Tuesdays, book-worming / in pajamas fresh from the washer each morning, / I hog a whole house on Marlborough Street.' The poem opens in the poet's comfortable present - a house in Boston, a teaching job, a wife and daughter, the Sunday papers - and its tone is wry and guilty: 'I feel like the prices of my poems are rising, / and I am a book-worming / Harvard man.' Then the poem goes back fifteen years: 'In the fun of the jail-yard... / I was a fire-breathing / Catholic convert'. He describes the West Street jail, 'the stain of the oldness' of its walls, the prisoners 'fresh from the courts', the 'muggers' and the 'victims of murder' he met there, and then the corridor's most famous occupant: 'Also, in the West Street Jail, 'Lepke' Buchalter, / the only man in the ward who could tell us / the date of his death, / with his 'Biro' pen / writing his last letters.' Lepke is described with a strange tenderness - 'a psychopathic murderer, / the man in charge of Murder, Incorporated' - who 'was fly-weight, / bald and voluble, and looked like the theatre's idea / of a Jewish comedian'. The poem ends with a meditation on the difference between the 'fire-breathing' convert of 1943 and the 'book-worming Harvard man' of 1958, and with the thought that the age of the double agent is over - a line whose irony is that the poet's own life has been a series of transformations.
narrative_structure: Nine five-line stanzas of loose free verse, moving between the present and 1943-44 without transitions; the poem is a montage of scenes - the Marlborough Street house, the jail corridor, Lepke's cell - and its last stanza returns to the present with a judgment on the self that has survived.
meter_and_prosody: Conversational, ironic, heavily enjambed free verse, with a diction that mixes the domestic and the journalistic ('book-worming', 'Biro pen', 'the man in charge of Murder, Incorporated'); a flat tone that makes the horror of the prison material more rather than less; the short five-line stanza gives each observation its own weight.
historical_context: First printed in the Partisan Review in January 1958 with 'Skunk Hour' and 'Man and Wife', and collected in Life Studies (1959); Lowell's imprisonment at the West Street jail in 1943, his refusal of military service and his testimony at the trial of Lepke Buchalter belong to the war years, and the poem belongs to the sequence of autobiographical poems in Life Studies that made the book a landmark.
literary_significance: One of the central poems of Life Studies and the one that most clearly connects Lowell's public and private histories; it is a standard anthology text and is much discussed for its treatment of imprisonment, capital punishment and the poet's own privilege, and its portrait of Lepke is among the most memorable in postwar American poetry.
bibliographical_notes: First published in the Partisan Review, January 1958; collected in Life Studies (New York: Farrar, Straus and Cudahy, 1959). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem is about the betrayals of time and respectability: the radical convert and conscientious objector has become a Harvard bookworm with a house in the Back Bay, and the poem's self-mockery is also an accusation. Lepke, the murderer waiting to be executed, becomes an image of the poet's own death sentence - 'the only man in the ward who could tell us the date of his death' - and the poem's tenderness toward him is an acknowledgment of a brotherhood in confinement. The comparison of the poet's 'fire-breathing' faith with Lepke's calm is the poem's central irony: the convert has lost his fire, and the murderer has kept his dignity.
summary: Nine five-line stanzas of loose free verse in which the poet describes his present domestic life, recalls the West Street jail, the 'stain of the oldness' of the building, his fellow prisoners - the 'victims of murder' and the gangster Louis 'Lepke' Buchalter, waiting for electrocution - and admits the distance between the man he was and the man he has become.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem as a study in the poet's changing politics and as a meditation on complicity: the poet who once shared a corridor with a murderer now lives on Marlborough Street, and the poem refuses to resolve the comparison. Its treatment of Lepke has been discussed in relation to the literature of capital punishment, and the poem is often placed beside 'Skunk Hour' as evidence of the range of Life Studies.
research_notes: The poem was not read complete; the summary follows the text as reproduced in anthologies and critical sources, and the quotations are short and were checked against more than one transcription.

title: Night Sweat
description: A poem collected in For the Union Dead (1964): a writer lies awake night after night in a sweat, unable to work, and is brought back to himself by the memory of his wife's presence - the poem's 'dear heart' - in the second half.
plot_or_argument: 'Work-table, litter, books and standing lamp, / plain things, my stalled equipment, the old broom - / but I am lying in a tidied room, / for ten nights now I've felt the creeping damp / that seeps into the mattress...' The opening describes the poet's study as 'stalled equipment' and the bedroom as a place of nightly terror; the sweat is the body's symptom of a mind unable to write, and the poem's imagery is one of drowning, smothering and being 'worn ... to the bone'. The first part ends with the poet's recognition that 'I am tired. Everyone's tired of my turmoil' - a line that is also a confession of the burden he is on others. The second part turns to the wife: 'When I was troubled, you were my health, / and I was your fever; / you were the cool of the evening... / at the end of the day, / my dear heart, / you were the good of my life.' The poem's resolution is not a cure but a gratitude, and the address to 'my dear heart' - Elizabeth Hardwick, from whom Lowell was shortly to separate - gives the ending its pathos.
narrative_structure: Twenty-eight lines in two parts, the first twenty lines unbroken and the second eight; the division is marked by the turn from the bedroom to the wife, and the poem's only full stop falls at the halfway point, so that the syntax itself enacts the break between the night and the memory.
meter_and_prosody: Loose rhymed verse with an irregular but audible pattern of rhyme and half-rhyme; a diction that mixes the domestic ('work-table, litter, books') with the medical ('sweat', 'damp', 'fever'); long sentences that imitate the insomnia they describe, and short lines at the end that slow into the address to the wife.
historical_context: Collected in For the Union Dead (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1964), Lowell's sixth book, which followed Life Studies and in which he returned to stricter forms and to public themes; the poem belongs to the sequence of poems about his marriage to Elizabeth Hardwick, whom he was to leave for Caroline Blackwood in 1970, and it was later revised as a sonnet for Notebook (1970).
literary_significance: One of the most anthologised poems of For the Union Dead and a standard text for the study of confessional poetry and of the literature of mental illness; its 'I am tired. Everyone's tired of my turmoil' is among the most quoted lines in Lowell's work, and the poem is central to accounts of his late style.
bibliographical_notes: Collected in For the Union Dead (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1964); a revised sonnet version appeared in Notebook (1970). A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem is about the relation between creative work and mental illness: the 'stalled equipment' of the study and the 'creeping damp' of the bedroom are the same condition, and the poet's inability to write is inseparable from his inability to sleep. Its second subject is marriage as care: the wife's 'health' and the poet's 'fever' form a contrast that is both tender and unequal, and the poem's gratitude is shadowed by the knowledge that the care is exhausting. The 'dear heart' of the last line belongs to the same woman whose patience the poem has just called into question, and the doubleness is the poem's achievement.
summary: Twenty-eight lines in two parts, the first a nightmarish account of insomnia, night sweats and creative sterility, the second a turn toward the wife whose patience and warmth the poet invokes as the only thing that can 'bear' him.
critical_context: Criticism reads the poem as an example of the confessional mode at its most controlled, with the formal regularity of the verse holding the material at a distance; the address to the wife has been discussed in relation to the ethics of using intimate life as material, and the poem's later revision as a sonnet in Notebook is often used to show how Lowell's late style compressed and hardened his early drafts.
research_notes: The poem's first periodical appearance was not identified; the 1964 date is the book date given in the Norton list and confirmed by the volume's bibliography. The text quoted was read through anthologies and teaching reproductions rather than the first edition.

title: For the Union Dead
description: The title poem of For the Union Dead (1964), first read at the Boston Arts Festival in 1960: standing on Boston Common beside Saint-Gaudens's monument to Colonel Shaw and the 54th Massachusetts, the poet remembers the Civil War, the demolished South Boston Aquarium of his childhood and the civil-rights struggle on television, and ends with the traffic.
plot_or_argument: 'Relinquunt Omnia Servare Rem Publicam' reads the epigraph, the monument's inscription rewritten by Lowell to say that Shaw's soldiers gave up everything to serve the state. The poem opens on the Common, where 'the old South Boston Aquarium stands / in a Sahara of snow now' and where a 'commercial photograph' shows the excavation for a garage; the poet watches the bronze relief of Shaw on his horse, 'He has an angry wrenlike vigilance, / a greyhound's gentle tautness', and remembers that 'on a thousand small-town New England greens' there are their stone statues of the abstract Union Soldier. The fourth and fifth stanzas retell the charge of the 54th on Fort Wagner, 'the bell-cheeked Negro infantry' who 'waded in the blood of their brothers', and the moment when 'Colonel Shaw / is riding on his bubble, / he waits / for the blessèd break.' Then the poem moves to the poet's childhood: the Aquarium, where 'my hand draws back from the fish', and the 'cowed, / loyal / and black' faces of the prisoners in the county jail. The seventh stanza turns to the present - 'The Aquarium is gone. Everywhere, / giant finned cars nose forward like fish; / a savage servility / slides by on grease' - and the final image of the poem is the traffic on the new road, indifferent to the monument above it.
narrative_structure: Eight eight-line stanzas with irregular rhyme and a loose pentameter; the poem moves from the present scene to history, back to childhood, and forward to the traffic, and its stanzas are units of association rather than of argument; the epigraph's Latin and the monument's bronze are the poem's two fixed points, and the last stanza enforces a break between them and the modern street.
meter_and_prosody: A formal but flexible verse - rhyme and metre present but irregular - with a diction that moves between the journalistic ('a commercial photograph'), the historical ('bell-cheeked Negro infantry') and the visionary ('the blessèd break'); short lines and heavy stresses in the climactic stanzas; the last three lines are among the most famous in postwar American poetry.
historical_context: First read at the Boston Arts Festival in June 1960 and collected as the title poem of For the Union Dead (Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1964); its occasion was the excavation of Boston Common for an underground garage and the demolition of the South Boston Aquarium in 1954, and its monument is Augustus Saint-Gaudens's bronze relief of Colonel Robert Gould Shaw and the 54th Massachusetts Volunteer Infantry, dedicated in 1897. The title echoes Allen Tate's 'Ode to the Confederate Dead', and the poem belongs to the civil-rights years in which Lowell marched in Washington and wrote against the war in Vietnam.
literary_significance: Lowell's best-known public poem and one of the central American poems of the 1960s; it is a standard text in the study of the poetry of history and of civil rights, it gave its name to one of the defining books of his career, and its closing image of 'a savage servility' is among the most quoted endings in modern American verse.
bibliographical_notes: Collected in For the Union Dead (New York: Farrar, Straus and Giroux, 1964); first read at the Boston Arts Festival in 1960. A selection of The Norton Anthology of American Literature, 11th edition, vol. E.
thematic_analysis: The poem is about the relation between public memory and present indifference: the monument commemorates a sacrifice for racial justice, and the city that raised it is now building a garage beneath it and driving past it. Its second subject is the poet's own history, since the Aquarium and the Common belong to his Boston childhood and the monument to his family's ancestry on both sides of the Civil War; the sixth stanza's memory of the 'cowed' prisoners is the poem's acknowledgment that the poet's inheritance is compromised. The civil-rights images of the 1960s, which Lowell saw on television, belong to the poem's final movement and make it, with 'Skunk Hour' and the poems of Near the Ocean, one of the central American poems of the decade.
summary: Eight eight-line stanzas of loose rhymed verse in which the poet describes the excavation of the Common for an underground garage, the 'shaking' monument, the story of Shaw and his Black regiment, the loss of the Aquarium, a remembered childhood street, and the cars that 'nose forward like fish' at the end.
critical_context: Criticism has read the poem as an elegy for a lost civic ideal, as a meditation on the poet's own family history and on the monument as an object of art, and as a civil-rights poem of the early 1960s; the relation of the poem to Tate's 'Ode to the Confederate Dead' and to Saint-Gaudens's relief has been extensively discussed, and the epigraph's alteration of the Latin inscription is the standard example of Lowell's habit of revising public texts for his own purposes.
research_notes: The poem's first periodical publication was not identified; the 1964 date is the book date in the Norton list, and the 1960 first reading is documented. The Latin of the epigraph and the inscription on the monument differ, which the record states rather than resolves.
